checkpoints: Redis Cluster partitions the keyspace into 16384 hash slots and, by default, computes a key's slot as `CRC16(key) mod 16384` over the entire key string.

Three unrelated key names such as `quota:u:<userId>`, `quota:t:<tenantId>`, and `quota:g` share no common substring, so they almost certainly hash to different slots and can even be owned by different nodes.

A Lua script executed via `EVALSHA`/`EVAL` is only allowed to touch keys that all resolve to the same slot, because Redis needs that guarantee to run the script atomically and single-threaded on one node without cross-node coordination.

When keys span multiple slots, Redis Cluster rejects the command outright with `CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot`, which is exactly why the endpoint 500s on every call once deployed to a cluster.

Standalone Redis has no concept of hash slots — every key lives on the same single node — so a multi-key script over `quota:u:*`, `quota:t:*`, and `quota:g` works there by accident, not because the key naming is correct.

A hash-tag fixes this by wrapping the substring the keys should share — here the tenant id — in curly braces, e.g. `` `{q:${tenantId}}:u:${userId}` ``, `` `{q:${tenantId}}:t` ``, `` `{q:${tenantId}}:g` ``.

Redis Cluster's slot-hashing rule has a special case: when a key contains a `{...}` substring, only the text inside the first pair of braces is hashed, so all three keys sharing the same braced tag land on the same slot and node and the multi-key script becomes atomic again.

Forcing all of a tenant's keys onto a single slot via a shared hash-tag concentrates that tenant's entire quota traffic onto one node, so a very large tenant can turn that node into a hot spot; the standard mitigation is to sub-shard the tag (e.g. append a bucket to the tag) for such tenants, at the cost that cross-bucket state for that tenant is no longer atomic in a single script.
